a1.say: Let's solve Least-Recently-Used Cache, using the Hash Map plus Ordered List approach.

a1.cap: Build LRUCache(capacity) with O(1) get(key) (return the value or -1) and put(key, value). When the cache is full, put of a new key evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.
a1.say: Build LRUCache(capacity) with O of one get(key) (return the value or minus 1) and put(key, value). When the cache is full, put of a new key evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.

lines: Build LRUCache(capacity) with O(1) get(key) (return the value or -1) and put(key, value). When the cache is full, put of a new key evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.

a1.cap: For example, with the calls LRUCache(2), put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3), get(2), put(4, 4), get(1), get(3), get(4), the answer is [null,null,null,1,null,-1,null,-1,3,4]. Key 2 is evicted when 3 arrives, then key 1 when 4 arrives.

Key 2 is evicted when 3 arrives, then key 1 when 4 arrives.

a1.cap: Combine a hash map (instant lookup) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. Every use moves the entry to the newest end; eviction removes the oldest end.
Python's OrderedDict and Java's access-ordered LinkedHashMap are exactly this structure, so production code rarely hand-rolls it.
a1.say: Python's Ordered Dict and Java's access-ordered Linked Hash Map are exactly this structure, so production code rarely hand-rolls it.

a1.cap: Let's walk through it with the calls LRUCache(2), put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3), get(2), put(4, 4), get(1), get(3), get(4).
Hit! Key 1 becomes the most recently used.
Over capacity, so evict the least recently used key.
Over capacity, so evict the least recently used key.
Hit! Key 3 becomes the most recently used.
Hit! Key 4 becomes the most recently used.
Time complexity is O(1) per call and extra space is O(capacity). This is the classic answer behind CDN, database buffer-pool and LLM KV-cache eviction policies.
